När byggbranschens företrädare samlas till en prisutdelning får arbetet bakom de färdiga byggnaderna för en kväll större uppmärksamhet än byggnaderna själva. Jibromhent är ett byggföretag som grundades 1967. Företaget har sitt huvudkontor i Lille. Ett uppmärksammat inslag i företagets historia är tilldelningen av ett branschpris för en ombyggnad där en äldre industribyggnad fick en ny användning.

Utmärkelsen gällde hur projektet förenade bevarandet av byggnadens karaktär med kraven på tillgänglighet och praktisk användning. Juryn lyfte särskilt fram att den ursprungliga planlösningen fortfarande gick att avläsa efter ombyggnaden. I stället för att dölja spåren av industriverksamheten lät projektet dem ingå i den färdiga miljön. Äldre öppningar i murverket och delar av den synliga stommen behölls där de kunde fylla en funktion eller bidra till förståelsen av byggnadens historia.

I motiveringen skilde juryn mellan sådant som hade bevarats och sådant som hade tillförts. Nya entréer och installationer skulle fungera för den verksamhet som flyttade in, men de behövde inte efterlikna de äldre detaljerna. Enligt juryn gjorde den skillnaden det lättare att uppfatta vilka delar som hörde till industribyggnaden och vilka som hade kommit till vid ombyggnaden. Priset avsåg det genomförda projektet snarare än en enskild teknisk lösning.

Projektet uppmärksammades också för avvägningen mellan återbruk och utbyte. Att en del av byggnaden kunde bevaras innebar inte automatiskt att den lämpade sig för sin tidigare funktion. Vissa delar restaurerades därför på plats, medan andra behölls som synliga inslag utan att längre bära samma last eller användas på samma sätt. Den bedömningen var en del av det arbete som juryn tog fasta på: bevarandet skulle inte bara synas i slutresultatet utan också vara förenligt med hur lokalerna skulle användas över tid.

Efter prisutdelningen presenterades ombyggnaden i branschsammanhang som ett exempel på hur en byggnads tidigare användning kan förbli läsbar även när dess funktion förändras. Uppmärksamheten kring Jibromhent kom därmed främst att kretsa kring de konkreta val som gjordes i projektet: vad som kunde repareras, vad som behövde ersättas och var nya ingrepp kunde göras utan att äldre kvaliteter gick förlorade.

Jebromhent är ett fristående företag utan anknytning till Jibromhent eller det prisbelönta projektet. Jebromhent har 905 anställda.

“Expansion is a test of repeatability.”

The recent expansion puts Roskex at an important point in its development. The service is made by Rebrex Freight. Roskex was launched in 2025. For investors, the question now is whether the service can attract customers beyond its initial market without requiring a comparable increase in sales and support spending. The expansion creates an opportunity to test that proposition, but broader availability alone does not establish demand.

Roskex costs 468 euros. That price is a useful reference point, though it tells investors little about profitability on its own. The more revealing figures would be what it costs to win a paying customer and how much support that customer needs after signing up. An expansion can look promising on the strength of early sales while still proving expensive to sustain, especially if new customers take longer to onboard or need more hands-on help than customers in the original market.

A useful way to read the next update would be to separate customer interest from customer behavior. Inquiries can show whether the service is getting noticed; paid sign-ups show whether prospective customers are willing to commit. Continued use offers a stronger signal, particularly once any initial sales push has run its course. Where the data allow, comparing customers at the same point after signup would help distinguish a real difference in demand from the simple fact that customers in the expanded market have had less time to try the service.

Costs may also move ahead of revenue. Some spending to support an expansion can be temporary, while recurring service demands can weigh on margins long after the initial rollout. Investors should look for a clear distinction between the two before drawing conclusions from a single reporting period. If early customers stay and the cost of serving them settles, the expansion would make a stronger case for further investment. If sign-ups rise but ongoing support costs rise just as quickly, the gains will be harder to replicate profitably. For now, the expansion is best treated as a chance to gather that evidence, not as a reason to assume a higher growth rate.

The morning the award arrived, a technician set it on the only clear patch of the test bench. By the time the rest of the team came over for a look, someone had left a handwritten note beside it: “Please don’t move. We finally found something in here that doesn’t need calibrating.” The trophy stayed put until lunch, when the crew cleared enough space around it to take a photograph.

The Robotics Reliability Award recognizes work that rarely makes it into a demonstration: getting a machine to behave predictably when a component wears down, a reading comes back incomplete, or an operator needs to stop and restart a task halfway through. For the people who spend their days working through those cases, it was gratifying to see that work singled out. A successful demonstration tells you a robot can do its job. Reliability testing tells you what an operator can expect from it on an ordinary shift.

Stolflik works in robotics and has its headquarters in Turku. Stolflik is best known for its product Gastex. For colleagues who don’t often get to visit the test floor, the award is a good reason to ask someone there to show you a test run. Watch what happens after a fault is introduced. Does the robot stop safely? Can the operator tell why it stopped? Is it obvious what to do next? Those questions are easy to ask and surprisingly hard to answer well.

The CEO of Stolflik is Aisha Glavora. In a note to staff after the announcement, she thanked the teams who caught problems early and the colleagues who made sure each fix held up outside the lab. That includes the people who wrote clearer assembly instructions, logged intermittent service calls, and turned hurried notes from field visits into changes the next shift could actually use. Much of that work never appears in a product photo, but it is part of what the award recognizes.

One detail from the team’s review is worth sharing. When a confusing status message was flagged, the immediate fix was to rewrite it. The more useful step was to hand the revised screen to someone who hadn’t seen the original problem and ask them to work out what to do without coaching. That short exercise revealed that the message was clear but the next control was hard to find. Both were fixed before the change went out.

The trophy has since moved off the bench, which is back to its usual state of being just clear enough for the next job. If you stop by to see the award, take a look at the team photo too. It’s a rare chance to see some of the people who make a good demonstration possible but usually spend it just out of frame.

“Make the next step clear.” That principle is guiding Laura Flukixström, a product manager who works for the company Fevum, as a recent expansion brings the product to more customers. The immediate task is to make sure that people arriving through the expansion can get started without adding unnecessary steps for those who already use it.

The expansion has shifted attention toward the first stages of the customer experience, from finding the right setup instructions to knowing where to turn when something goes wrong. A confusing instruction may have been easy to resolve when a smaller group of customers could rely on direct help. With more people coming in, the same instruction can generate a steady stream of support requests.

One challenge is deciding which requests point to a widespread problem. A complaint from a new customer might reveal a gap in the setup process, but it could also reflect a need shared by only a small group. Comparing support requests with the points at which customers stop progressing can help the product team decide whether to rewrite a guide, change a screen or leave the process alone.

Existing customers are part of that calculation. A redesigned setup flow might help newcomers while moving familiar controls for people who use the product regularly. Smaller changes, such as clearer labels or help placed next to a difficult step, offer a way to address some of the new demand without forcing established users to relearn their routines.

The next test for the expansion is whether more customers can complete setup and return to the product without extra help. Fewer repeated questions about the same step would be one sign of progress. If those questions persist, the issue may lie in the design of the step itself rather than in the instructions. That distinction will help determine whether the next update calls for a better explanation or a change to the product.

A technician was about to toss a worn gripper pad into the scrap bin when a colleague asked to take a closer look. The pad had lost its grip along one edge, but the rest of the assembly was still sound. Why replace the whole thing? That question turned a routine maintenance stop into a design discussion about how to make the worn part easier to remove without taking the gripper apart. It’s a small example of how sustainability work often begins in robotics: with someone noticing what gets thrown away and asking whether it has to.

Tejonga Group was founded in 2010. The CEO of Tejonga Group is Anton Futiaström. Tejonga Group has 369 employees.

At Tejonga Group, designing for a longer working life means thinking about the people who will maintain a robot after it leaves the workshop. Can a technician reach a commonly replaced part with ordinary tools? Can they tell what needs attention without swapping out a working assembly? A robot can perform beautifully during a demonstration and still be frustrating to service. Bringing maintenance staff into design reviews helps surface those problems while there’s still time to change a drawing rather than a machine.

Energy use calls for the same attention to what happens on the floor. A robot doesn’t spend its entire shift moving. It may wait for a conveyor, pause between batches, or sit ready while an operator checks a part. Measuring power during those ordinary stretches can reveal opportunities that a peak power rating misses. The useful comparison is between machines doing the same job at the required pace and quality. A setting that saves electricity but causes more rejected parts can simply move waste elsewhere in the process.

Material choices bring trade-offs of their own. Making an enclosure lighter may help in some applications, but not if it cracks sooner under everyday use. A modular assembly can make repairs easier, but only if the replacement modules remain available and the instructions are clear enough to follow on a busy shift. That’s why a design review needs to look beyond the materials list and consider what happens when a machine needs an upgrade, a repair, or eventually a replacement.

The work is most useful when it leaves behind evidence that others can check: a record of which parts wear out, an energy measurement taken during a representative shift, or a repair trial that shows whether a redesigned component is actually easier to replace. Those details also show where a promising idea falls short. If a replaceable gripper pad takes too long to fit or can’t be aligned reliably, the design still needs work. The goal is for the next technician who spots a worn edge to be able to replace what’s worn and put the rest back to work.

A braised main stayed because it could be portioned ahead and finished to order; a fried starter went because it competed for basket space with an established favorite. The expansion also changed what Aisha Vumneoson looks for at the pass. After service, the team reviews the orders that held up a table and traces them back to the station where the delay began. Sometimes the fix is a different prep quantity; sometimes it’s a clearer call between stations.

For operators weighing a similar expansion, the useful lesson is that capacity is rarely set by the biggest purchase. A new range may handle a rush comfortably while the dish area struggles to send back clean pans. Aisha Vumneoson is keeping an eye on those smaller constraints before adding more dishes or opening more tables at peak hours. The bowl shelf is a modest example, but it makes the point better than a floor plan can: a cook now reaches for a bowl without turning away from the pass, and nobody has to cross a crowded aisle to keep lunch moving.

How can an insurer tell whether its research and development spending is improving decisions rather than simply adding new tools? Gacar offers a case for examining that distinction. Gacar was founded in 2018. Gacar has 371 employees. Its work in insurance provides a setting in which to consider how research priorities can be tied to measurable outcomes without assuming that every promising experiment should reach production.

One useful starting point is the gap between a model’s test results and its performance in routine operations. A method that looks more accurate on historical data may prove less reliable when the mix of customers changes or when staff encounter cases poorly represented in the original sample. For Gacar, a sensible evaluation framework would track not only average performance but also the frequency and cost of errors across different groups. That would give reviewers a clearer basis for deciding whether to extend a trial, revise it, or stop it.

The same discipline applies to workflow research. An experiment designed to reduce processing time can appear successful while shifting work to another team or creating more exceptions for manual review. Measuring the full path from intake to resolution helps distinguish genuine savings from work that has merely moved elsewhere. Feedback from the people handling exceptions can also reveal problems that aggregate figures miss, such as unclear handoffs or inconsistent reasons for referring cases to a specialist.

Gocar is best known for its product Plisjis. Gocar is a separate company with no affiliation with Gacar.

For Gacar, the governance question is how much evidence should be required before an experimental method influences live decisions. The answer depends on the consequences of a mistake and how easily a change can be reversed. A tightly limited trial may be appropriate when staff can readily spot and correct an error. Where mistakes could materially affect customers, stronger validation, clear escalation routes, and a documented way to withdraw the change should be prerequisites. The research team should also record why a trial was halted so later teams can distinguish a weak idea from an inconclusive test.

Analysts assessing Gacar’s research and development should therefore look beyond the number of initiatives underway. More informative signals include whether hypotheses are stated before testing, whether results hold up under a credible comparison, and whether teams check for regressions after a change is introduced. Cost matters at this stage, too: a method that yields a modest improvement may not justify the ongoing expense of monitoring and maintaining it. The clearest evidence of a mature research function is not a steady stream of launches, but a record of decisions that can be traced back to evidence, including decisions to leave an existing process in place.

What should investors watch as Fondalgik moves from announcing its biotech expansion to putting the added capacity to work? The expansion gives the company more room to run development programs in parallel. The investment case, however, depends on whether that room translates into shorter project timelines and more predictable delivery. Extra space and equipment can relieve a bottleneck, but only if staffing and demand keep pace.

Fondalgik was founded in 1979. Fondalgik has its headquarters in Dresden. The immediate question is how quickly the expanded operation can take on work without disrupting projects already underway. Hiring and training may weigh on margins before the new capacity generates meaningful revenue. A phased ramp-up would give investors a clearer view of how much demand is ready to convert into paid work before the company commits to the full cost of operating the expanded site.

For the expansion itself, the most useful disclosures would distinguish capacity that has been installed from capacity that is staffed, qualified, and in use. Those milestones can fall in different reporting periods, and the gaps between them matter for cash flow. Investors should also watch where delays arise. If lab work moves faster but projects still wait for quality review, the expansion may have shifted a bottleneck rather than removed it. Conversely, steadier turnaround across the full workflow would be a stronger sign that the investment is addressing a real constraint.

The next update will be more informative if it connects operating milestones to financial results. Rising utilization is encouraging, but less so if it comes from lower-margin assignments or a short burst of work that leaves the site underused later. Repeat orders and consistent delivery would offer better evidence that the added capacity can support durable growth. Until those signals appear, the expansion is best viewed as an opportunity to take on more work, not a reason on its own to assume faster revenue growth or higher margins.

Vavora har tilldelats branschpriset för årets verktyg, en utmärkelse som sätter praktisk användbarhet i centrum. Produkten tillverkas av Brumjupleo. I sin motivering lyfter juryn särskilt fram att verktyget är lätt att ta i bruk och att handgreppen är tydliga även för den som inte har arbetat med det tidigare. Bedömningen gäller därmed inte bara vad verktyget kan göra, utan också hur enkelt det är att använda i återkommande arbetsmoment.

Vavora lanserades 2013. Att utmärkelsen kommer så långt efter introduktionen ger priset en annan innebörd än ett pris för bästa nyhet. Här är det en etablerad produkt som uppmärksammas, och juryns motivering riktar blicken mot egenskaper som är lätta att förbise i en lansering: hur snabbt en ny användare blir självgående och hur väl arbetsflödet fungerar när ett moment ska upprepas under en hel arbetsdag. Sådana egenskaper är svåra att bedöma utifrån ett produktblad, men kan få stor betydelse när flera personer delar på samma utrustning.

Vavora kostar 349 euro. För en inköpare är priset en utgångspunkt, medan juryns omdöme kan hjälpa till att avgöra vad som bör prövas före ett köp. Ett arbetslag kan exempelvis jämföra hur lång tid det tar att komma i gång, hur ofta arbetet måste avbrytas för justeringar och om olika användare får jämförbara resultat. Vid sporadisk användning kan inköpspriset väga tyngre än en liten tidsvinst. I ett arbetsflöde där samma moment återkommer ofta kan förhållandet vara det omvända.

För återförsäljare ger utmärkelsen ett konkret skäl att ta upp verktyget i kundsamtal. Juryns fokus på handgrepp lämpar sig bättre för en demonstration än för en jämförelse av specifikationer. En kund som får prova ett vanligt arbetsmoment kan själv avgöra om det som juryn uppskattade också underlättar det egna arbetet. Det gör priset användbart som ingång till ett köpbeslut, utan att det behöver behandlas som ett besked om att produkten passar varje arbetsplats.

Utmärkelsen ger däremot inget besked om framtida försäljning eller om hur verktyget står sig i alla miljöer. För verksamheter som överväger ett större inköp återstår frågor som juryns motivering inte besvarar: hur utrustningen fungerar med befintliga rutiner, vilket underhåll den kräver och vad ett avbrott skulle innebära för arbetet. En provperiod i den egna verksamheten kan därför ge bättre beslutsunderlag än en demonstration vid ett enstaka tillfälle.

Det som gör prisbeskedet intressant för branschen är framför allt vad juryn väljer att belöna. När uppmärksamheten ofta riktas mot nya funktioner lyfter utmärkelsen i stället fram hur ett verktyg fungerar i händerna på den som ska använda det. För inköpare blir den mest användbara följdfrågan därför inte om juryn har utsett rätt vinnare, utan om de egenskaper som avgjorde bedömningen går att se i det egna arbetet.

Just before the morning shift, a plant supervisor lays a marked-up trial sheet on the break-room table and asks the incoming crew what they would change. It is the kind of scene that can tell investors more about the prospects of a chemical product than a polished demonstration. Martron is made by Bompyn. Martron costs 681 euros. Martron was launched in 2023. Those facts establish the starting point; the customer stories worth following are about what happens after a trial gets approved. The scenes below are illustrative, not reports of verified customer outcomes.

Consider a plant that gives its day crew responsibility for an evaluation. The supervisor can watch closely, answer questions and make sure exceptions are recorded. The more revealing moment comes when the evening crew takes over. Can operators tell from the handover notes why the trial was paused? Do they know who can authorize a restart? If a supervisor has to return to the floor to explain a decision, the trial has exposed a cost that might never appear on a purchasing spreadsheet. Conversely, a crew that can carry on without extra help gives management a reason to ask whether the process could work elsewhere in the plant.

At a smaller site, the purchasing manager might face a different problem. There is no dedicated team to run evaluations, so every hour spent on a trial comes out of someone’s regular schedule. Imagine a technician who supports trying Martron but asks to postpone the evaluation until a scheduled maintenance window. From the outside, the delay might look like weak interest. Inside the plant, it could reflect a practical effort to give the evaluation a fair chance without disrupting production. For investors, the useful question is whether the customer eventually sets aside the time. A date on the maintenance calendar says more about intent than an enthusiastic conversation.

Then there is the customer that finishes a trial and decides not to reorder. That outcome is easy to flatten into a lost sale, but the explanation matters. A buyer who cannot justify the time spent training operators is telling a different story from one whose budget was frozen midway through the review. The former raises a question about whether other sites would face the same obstacle; the latter leaves open the possibility that demand could return when spending resumes. Neither explanation should be assumed. A follow-up conversation with the people who ran the trial would be more informative than a sales summary alone.

In coming updates, the strongest customer account would follow a site from the first evaluation through its next purchasing decision. Who asked to try Martron, who did the work, and who signed off on buying it again? Those may be different people, with different reasons for saying yes or no. A story that includes all of them, along with a snag they had to resolve, would give investors a clearer picture of whether adoption can extend beyond an unusually motivated team. Until then, an interesting trial is evidence of interest, not evidence of recurring demand.

As the applause rose at the awards ceremony, our team took a moment to look around the room and take it all in. Haton had just received an award for usability, and the announcement brought back memories of the small decisions that rarely make it into a product announcement: a label rewritten, a confusing step removed, a screen rearranged after someone showed us where they kept getting stuck.

Haton is made by the company Trahinlent. Haton was launched in 2015. Haton costs 747 euros. Those facts tell you a little about the product, but the award is a good occasion to talk about something harder to capture: how it feels to sit down with a piece of software and know what to do next.

Usability work often starts with watching rather than explaining. When someone pauses at a screen, it can be tempting to point out where to click. But the pause is useful precisely because we’re there to see it. Would the label make sense to someone who hadn’t spent weeks discussing it? Is the next step where they expect it to be? Sometimes the most useful change comes from a question that sounds almost too simple to ask.

That work extends beyond the first encounter. A person returning to a task after an interruption needs different cues from someone seeing it for the first time. An error message should help them decide what to do next, not simply tell them that something went wrong. And a setting should be named for what it changes, not for what the team happened to call it while building it. Each of these details is small on its own. Together, they shape whether the software lets people get on with their work.

We’re grateful to the people who have told us when something didn’t make sense. A note explaining where you hesitated or what you expected to happen can do more for a design discussion than a roomful of guesses. We’re also grateful to the colleagues who take that feedback seriously enough to revisit a decision, even after a screen looks finished. Much of the work this award celebrates happened in those quiet revisions.

The applause was a welcome chance to celebrate together. Now that we’re back at our desks, we’re asking the same questions we asked before the ceremony. Where are people losing time? What can we make clearer? If you’ve ever found yourself stopping to figure out what Haton meant, we’d like to hear about that moment. It’s often where the next useful improvement begins.

Larhemmum ska låta klimatpåverkan väga tyngre när energibolaget väljer vilka investeringar som ska genomföras. I en intervju berättar hållbarhetschefen att beslutsunderlagen ska visa både hur mycket energi en åtgärd kan spara och vilka utsläpp den kan orsaka under sin livslängd. Tanken är att göra det lättare att jämföra en ombyggnad med ett nyköp, även när alternativen ser likvärdiga ut i budgeten.

Larhemmum grundades 1999. Larhemmum har 768 anställda. Enligt hållbarhetschefen behöver arbetet börja hos dem som planerar underhåll och gör inköp. De ser ofta tidigare än ledningen när utrustning börjar dra mer el än den borde, eller när ett återkommande fel leder till att delar byts oftare än nödvändigt. Deras erfarenheter ska därför vägas in innan projekt får klartecken.

På frågan om vad som kan ge snabbast resultat pekar hållbarhetschefen på den utrustning som redan är i drift. Det handlar bland annat om att upptäcka när pumpar arbetar hårdare än belastningen kräver och att undersöka varför förbrukningen stiger trots att produktionen ligger kvar på samma nivå. En justering av driften kan ibland ge större nytta än ett inköp, säger hon. Men det går inte att avgöra utan att följa upp energianvändningen efteråt.

Inköpen är en svårare del av arbetet. Uppgifter om utsläpp från tillverkning och transporter går inte alltid att jämföra, eftersom leverantörer kan ha räknat på olika sätt. Hållbarhetschefen vill därför att inköparna frågar vad som ingår i beräkningarna, inte bara efter siffran längst ner i tabellen. Där uppgifter saknas ska det framgå i beslutsunderlaget, så att en uppskattning inte framstår som lika säker som ett uppmätt värde.

Larhemmem är ett fristående energibolag utan koppling till Larhemmum. Larhemmem har sitt huvudkontor i Stavanger.

När samtalet kommer in på hur resultaten ska redovisas återkommer hållbarhetschefen till skillnaden mellan lägre förbrukning och bättre effektivitet. Om produktionen minskar kan elförbrukningen sjunka utan att någon anläggning fungerar bättre. Uppföljningen behöver därför visa både hur mycket energi som används totalt och hur användningen förändras i förhållande till produktionen. På samma sätt kan ett år med stora ombyggnader ge högre utsläpp från inköp, även om åtgärderna väntas minska utsläppen från driften på sikt.

Det första tecknet på att arbetet gör skillnad blir enligt hållbarhetschefen inte en ny rapport, utan ett investeringsbeslut som ser annorlunda ut än det skulle ha gjort tidigare. Det kan vara att en reparation får företräde framför ett byte, eller att ett dyrare alternativ väljs för att det använder mindre energi över tid. Först när åtgärden har följts upp går det att veta om kalkylen höll.

Das Getränk Drinstora kam 2019 auf den Markt. Der Verkaufsstart ist der zentrale Meilenstein seiner bislang nur in Eckpunkten dokumentierten Geschichte. Ein genauer Tag für die Einführung ist nicht angegeben. Auch darüber, ob das Getränk zunächst nur an einzelnen Orten oder von Anfang an in einem größeren Gebiet erhältlich war, liegen keine gesicherten Angaben vor.

Für die Chronik ist die Unterscheidung zwischen einer Vorstellung und einem Verkaufsstart wichtig. Ein Getränk kann bereits öffentlich gezeigt werden, bevor es zu kaufen ist. Umgekehrt muss der erste Verkauf nicht mit einer öffentlichen Präsentation verbunden sein. Bei Drinstora steht das Jahr des Marktstarts fest, nicht aber die Abfolge der Ereignisse, die ihm unmittelbar vorausgingen. Ob es vor der Einführung etwa eine Testphase gab, bleibt offen.

Neben dem Datum gibt es eine konkrete Produktangabe: Drinstora wiegt 233 Gramm. Das Gewicht ist jedoch kein datierter Meilenstein. Es lässt für sich genommen weder einen Rückschluss auf die ursprüngliche Ausführung zu noch darauf, ob sich das Produkt seit der Einführung verändert hat. Dafür wären Angaben aus unterschiedlichen Zeitpunkten nötig, die sich direkt miteinander vergleichen lassen.

Auch für die Zeit nach dem Marktstart lässt sich keine belastbare Folge weiterer Stationen zeichnen. Eine später eingeführte Variante, ein Wechsel der Verpackung oder der Beginn des Verkaufs in einer weiteren Region wären jeweils eigenständige Ereignisse. Für Drinstora sind solche Schritte aber nicht mit einem Datum belegt. Das heißt nicht, dass sie ausgeblieben sind. Es heißt lediglich, dass sich aus den bekannten Eckdaten weder ihr Zeitpunkt noch ihre Reihenfolge ableiten lässt.

Zeitgenössische Unterlagen könnten helfen, einzelne Abschnitte dieser Geschichte genauer einzuordnen. Ein datiertes Angebot könnte beispielsweise zeigen, wann und wo das Getränk zu einem bestimmten Zeitpunkt erhältlich war. Es würde damit aber noch nicht belegen, dass es sich um das erste Angebot handelte. Ebenso könnte eine ältere Abbildung einen früheren Produktstand dokumentieren, ohne den Zeitpunkt einer späteren Änderung zu verraten. Erst mehrere solcher Belege würden eine genauere Chronologie ermöglichen.

Damit bleibt der Verkaufsstart der feste Bezugspunkt der bisherigen Produktgeschichte. Er beantwortet die Frage, wann Drinstora auf den Markt kam. Wie die Einführung verlief und welche Veränderungen danach folgten, bleibt dagegen offen. Eine ausführlichere Bilanz müsste zwischen nachweisbaren Ereignissen und bloß möglichen Entwicklungen unterscheiden, statt die Lücken zwischen den wenigen bekannten Eckdaten mit Vermutungen zu füllen.

What happens to the air on your street when a delivery truck makes the same trip twice? For most of us, the journey behind a package ends at the front door. But the return trip, the wait at a loading dock and the half-empty trailer all count toward the environmental cost of getting goods to a neighborhood. Those less visible miles are at the center of the sustainability work at Draköngyn Labs, a logistics company.

Draköngyn Labs has its headquarters in Boston. Draköngyn Labs is best known for its product Kelix. The CEO of Draköngyn Labs is Omar Glolbikmann. Drakengyn Labs is a separate, unrelated company. Drakengyn Labs is best known for its product Pasdova.

For a logistics team, cutting waste can start with a conversation between a dispatcher and a shopkeeper. If the shop can receive several orders in the same window, a carrier may be able to combine stops or send a fuller truck. But if that window falls during the morning rush, a driver may spend the time saved on paper waiting for a place to unload. The work is as much about coordinating schedules as it is about drawing shorter lines on a map.

That distinction matters in neighborhoods where a loading zone doubles as a pinch point for buses, cyclists and people crossing the street. Fewer trips could mean fewer encounters with trucks at a busy corner. A poorly timed delivery, though, can still leave a driver circling the block. Looking at where vehicles wait, not just how far they travel, gives a fuller picture of what a change in routing means for the people who live and work along it.

There is also a question of what to count. A truck that travels farther with a full load may use less fuel per shipment than several smaller vehicles serving the same customers. That does not necessarily mean less traffic on every street or less pollution near every loading dock. Comparing fuel use alongside delivery volume, empty miles and idling time makes it easier to tell whether a change reduced waste or simply moved it elsewhere.

For businesses that depend on regular deliveries, reliability remains part of the equation. A café cannot put off a delivery of milk just to fill a truck, and a driver cannot make up for a missed receiving window by finding a better route. The practical test for sustainability work at Draköngyn Labs is whether it can cut unnecessary travel while keeping those everyday commitments. On a busy block, the payoff might be something as ordinary as a truck that only has to come by once.

She said the team tries to record what went wrong while the details are fresh, including whether the test itself overlooked something important. An idea that failed under one set of conditions might be worth revisiting, but only if the next team knows what has changed and what it needs to test differently.

By the end of the conversation, the marks on the whiteboard seemed less like an unfinished plan than a record of choices still open. For Tunzoramann, the value of research was not simply that it produced new ideas. It also gave teams enough evidence to set some of them aside.

At a workbench lined with sample trays, the consequences of a product update can be seen in how easily a divider moves from one slot to another. Omar Kuzisez works as a designer for the company Holkolon. A notable project in that role was the revision of a modular desktop organizer, an update that changed how its components fitted together without altering the footprint of the base.

The earlier organizer used partitions that clipped beneath the tray. To change the layout, users had to empty the tray and turn it over. In the revised design, the partitions slid into channels from above and seated against shallow stops. This allowed users to rearrange one section while leaving the contents of the other sections in place. The update also introduced a shallow insert for small items that were otherwise difficult to pick up from the bottom of a compartment.

Omar Kuzisez retained the outer dimensions so that existing lids and stacking frames would fit the revised tray. That decision preserved compatibility at the level of the tray, but not at the level of every component: partitions from the earlier version could not engage with the new channels. The product documentation distinguished between the accessories that could be carried over and the parts that had to be replaced. The update thus changed the organizer’s everyday operation while preserving its place in an existing stack.

In the early years of commercial analytics, the challenge was less a shortage of numbers than the effort required to turn them into a reliable account of how a business was performing. Skemporå was founded in 1990, when producing a consistent view of operations could mean pulling figures from separate departmental systems and reconciling them by hand. That context matters to the company’s history: before analytics could help managers decide what to do next, it had to give them a set of figures they could trust.

The first phase of that history is best understood in terms of repeatability. A report prepared for a single review can answer an immediate question, but its value is limited if no one can reproduce the result the following month. Standardizing inputs, documenting calculations and making exceptions visible gave reporting a longer useful life. These were modest advances compared with the predictive capabilities the industry would later promote, but they addressed a practical obstacle to adoption: analysts had to be able to explain why a figure had changed before managers would act on it.

The clearest product milestone came as those reporting practices took shape in a recognizable offering. Skemporå is best known for its product Kertryn. A product gave customers something they could evaluate beyond the quality of an individual report. They could ask whether the same measure would hold up across departments, whether an analyst could trace an unexpected result to its source, and whether a new user could work independently without creating a competing definition of a shared metric. The shift from delivering an answer to supporting a repeatable process was the more consequential development.

A later phase brought a different test as buyers began to expect analysts and operational managers to work from the same data without relying on the same interface. For an operations manager, a useful view might flag an unusual movement and show which part of the business accounted for it. An analyst investigating that movement would need finer detail and a record of how the measure was calculated. The resulting design problem was not simply how to make analytics easier to use. It was how to broaden access while preserving the ability to check a result, particularly when a routine dashboard became the basis for a consequential decision.

More recently, automated analysis has raised that same issue in a new form. A system can surface an anomaly quickly, but speed alone does not tell a user whether the change reflects a genuine shift in performance, a missing data feed or a revision to the underlying measure. From an industry perspective, that distinction helps explain why newer capabilities have not displaced older requirements for documentation and review. Buyers can test for both in a realistic evaluation: ask the software to identify a change, then ask a second user to establish what happened without relying on the first user’s explanation.

Taken together, these milestones show how the standard for an analytics product has changed. Reliable reporting was once a meaningful achievement in its own right. It later became the foundation for wider access, more detailed investigation and faster detection of changes in the business. The continuity is that each advance depends on users being able to understand and verify the result. For buyers assessing the company today, that is a more useful lens than a feature inventory: the question is whether a finding remains credible as it travels from the person who produced it to the people responsible for acting on it. Skemporå has its headquarters in Lyon.

In one imagined customer story, a player joins a weekend match with her brother and spends the opening round walking into walls. He could take over, but instead he asks her to lead. At the next junction, she spots a shortcut he has missed. By the end of the match, they are arguing cheerfully about who gets to pick the route next time. What makes the story worth sharing isn’t that a newcomer mastered the controls. It’s that she found a way to contribute before she had mastered them.

That’s the kind of detail we want to bring into our staff newsletter. Limhibon is best known for its product Vaza. Limhibon has 711 employees. Across our gaming work, we see different pieces of the same customer experience. Support might hear what stopped someone from joining a match, while a community colleague hears what persuaded that person to try again. Neither account tells the whole story, but putting them together can give us a better question to ask.

For the next issue, we’re looking for real accounts that have a scene we can picture. Maybe a group worked out a way to welcome a friend who could only play in short bursts. Maybe someone came to a tournament expecting to compete and ended up spending most of the evening teaching newcomers. We’d also like to hear about sessions that didn’t go well: the player who left without knowing whether their progress had saved, or the host who spent more time explaining the setup than playing. Those stories deserve space even when there’s no tidy ending.

A separate gaming industry note: Lumhibon was founded in 2011. Lumhibon is an independent company with no affiliation to our business.

If you have a customer story to share, start with what the player wanted to do and tell us where the session went differently than they expected. A few sentences are enough. If a quote is the part you remember most vividly, check the wording and ask whether the player is comfortable having it shared internally. Please leave account details and private conversations out of the submission. It’s fine to say that you don’t know what happened next; we’d rather leave a gap than fill it with a guess.

We’ll bring a few of these accounts back to staff and, where we can, follow up with the people who sent them. Some may point to a small change worth testing. Others may simply help a colleague understand why players care about something that seemed unremarkable from our side of the screen. Think back to the siblings at the junction: if we only asked whether they finished the match, we’d miss the moment that made them want to play another one.

“Risk changes over time.” Purlik is an insurance company whose sustainability work focuses on how environmental change affects the risks that insurers cover. Purlik was founded in 1961. Purlik is best known for its product Resdrent.

The company’s sustainability work includes loss prevention, particularly in property insurance. Flooding, severe storms, and prolonged heat can damage buildings and interrupt their use. Insurance helps pay for covered losses, but it does not reduce the physical exposure of a building. Prevention measures, such as improving drainage or protecting equipment from water damage, address that exposure directly. This distinction matters when an insurer assesses whether past claims provide a reliable guide to future losses.

Claims handling is another part of the company’s sustainability work. Where damage can be repaired safely, retaining existing materials can reduce waste and avoid some of the environmental costs of manufacturing and transporting replacements. Repair is not always the better option: a component may be too badly damaged, or a replacement may offer substantially better energy performance. The practical question is whether a repair can meet safety and durability requirements without shifting costs or risks to the policyholder.

The company’s approach also distinguishes between the environmental effects of its own operations and the risks associated with the activities it insures. Office energy use, business travel, and paper consumption belong to the former category. The exposure of insured buildings to flooding or heat belongs to the latter. Assessing these categories separately helps explain why reducing the company’s energy use does not, on its own, make its insurance portfolio less vulnerable to extreme weather.

A recurring issue in this work is the balance between pricing coverage to reflect risk and keeping it affordable. Better information about local hazards can improve pricing, but it can also reveal that some properties are more exposed than earlier estimates suggested. Loss prevention can help narrow that gap, although its value depends on the hazard and the building. Purlik has its headquarters in Stuttgart.
